methodological_questions: How to define PNR failure from possession-level data?
How to define pull-up shot (play type, distance, context)?
How to compute lift as PPP difference?
What is the appropriate unit of analysis (team-game, team-season, defender)?
How to test the proportion of units with lift>0?
How to handle data sparsity when pull-ups are rare after PNR failures?
How to control for confounders like opponent defense, game state, and regression to the mean?
How to ensure median lift>2pp is meaningful across units?

historical_evidence.finding: A1 adaptation falsification found adapter PPP lift +0.0667 (n=205), neutral +0.0248, no_signal +0.1260, wrong_way +0.0111. The adapter lift declined or reversed when conditioned on scheme-vote confidence. The apparent effect was produced by a construction, selection, or labelling flaw.

Scheme labeling from matchup/PBP fields yielded confident label rates of only 14.9% (DET) and 3.3% (ORL); switches_on field was unpopulated. Small sample (n=67/60 possessions) and low label rates made the question untestable.

Within-game adaptation toward SHOULD counters improved PPP by +0.058 (n=508). Later records indicate the apparent lift was an artifact due to selection or regression to the mean; no-signal baseline was the highest PPP group.

failed_approaches.what_failed: labeling defensive schemes from matchup/PBP data to identify coverage context
failed_approaches.why: very low confident label rates (3.3–14.9%) and missing switches_on field; small sample size made reliable inference impossible

failed_approaches.what_failed: naive adaptation PPP lift test without correcting for selection or regression to the mean
failed_approaches.why: apparent effect was an artifact due to construction/selection/labelling flaws; wrong-way teams also showed lift and scheme-confidence gradient was opposite to prediction

failed_approaches.what_failed: within-game adaptation lift as evidence of counter effectiveness
failed_approaches.why: later analyses revealed the lift was artifact from selection/regression to the mean

evidence_establishes: Adaptation lift studies in basketball are highly susceptible to artifacts, especially when conditioning on a prior event (PNR failure) without rigorous adjustment for regression to the mean.
Direct labeling of defensive scheme context from available basketball data is unreliable and extremely sparse.
Small sample sizes and sparse exposure have plagued similar counter-adaptation analyses.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether the specific PNR fail→pull-up counter is testable.
Any prior estimate of pull-up lift after PNR failures or the proportion of units with positive lift.
That the claim is false; only that naive tests often produce spurious support.
own_inferences: Conditioning on a PNR failure (likely a low-scoring event) and then measuring pull-up PPP will induce regression to the mean, biasing lift upward.
Pull-up shot attempts are a sub-category of play types; after a PNR failure, they may be rare per game, leading to extreme sparsity in many units.
A requirement of ≥70% of units with lift>0 and a median lift >2 pp is a very strong claim that demands large, stable, and well-identified effects—conditions unlikely to be met.
The historical prevalence of artifacts in similar adaptation claims suggests that any observed positive lift is more likely to be an artifact than a true causal counter-strategy effect.
Even with careful design, the data may not provide enough power to reliably distinguish a small true effect from noise.
uncertainties: Precise operational definition of PNR failure (points = 0, turnover, defensive stop, or below average PPP).
Definition of pull-up shot (play type action code, shot distance cutoffs) and whether play-type labels are accurate enough to isolate pull-ups.
Choice of unit of analysis: team-game (many sparse units), team-season (few, more possessions but only ~30 per season), or defender-season (sparsest).
What constitutes the proper baseline for lift: overall pull-up PPP, pull-up PPP in similar game situations, or a model-based expected value.
How to handle multiple pull-up opportunities after a single failure event and time-decay.
Whether the required thresholds (70%, 2 pp) are realistic given observed effect sizes in basketball.

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence did not directly test this question, but it strongly shaped the risk assessment. Earlier adaptation lift studies were repeatedly identified as artifacts, largely due to regression to the mean and selection biases. Without this evidence, one might have been more optimistic about a naive PPP comparison. The retrieved findings confirm that a do_not_proceed decision is warranted and that any test would require rigorous controls for RTM and sparsity.

blocking_constraints.text: Units may have too few pull-up possessions after PNR failures to estimate lift precisely; even aggregating to team-season yields only ~90 units across all available seasons, limiting power for a 70% proportion test.
Pull-up attempts are a subset of play types; conditioning on a preceding PNR failure further restricts the number of qualifying possessions, making many units nearly empty.
Conditioning on a PNR failure selects low-scoring possessions; subsequent pull-up PPP will regress toward the mean, creating spurious positive lift.
Opponent defensive strength, game location, score differential, and time situation confound both the occurrence of a PNR failure and the success of a subsequent pull-up.
The classification of a possession as a pull-up may be noisy in play-by-play data; misclassification could dilute or create spurious effects.

prior_work.summary: No prior study examined PNR failure leading to pull-up as a league-wide counter. Related adaptation lift tests repeatedly produced artifacts, and scheme labelling from available data was found unreliable.

risks.text: The direct conditioning on a PNR failure will cause regression to the mean in pull-up PPP, generating a positive lift artifact even in the absence of any counter strategy.
The required number of units (e.g., team-seasons) is limited; power to detect whether >70% of units have positive lift is low, especially after adjusting for confounders.
Many units will have very few pull-up possessions after a PNR failure, leading to unstable lift estimates and high variance.
Omitting opponent quality, game state, and shot context will bias lift estimates upward or downward.
Misclassification of play types (e.g., pull-up vs. catch-and-shoot) could create differential measurement error and invalidate the lift metric.
Similar lift may appear after any negative outcome (e.g., a missed shot of any type), not specific to PNR failure, rendering the claim unfalsifiable without placebo tests.

design.estimand: Team-season average points per possession (PPP) on pull-up shot possessions that directly follow a PNR failure, minus the expected PPP for pull-up shots by that team in similar game states but not preceded by a PNR failure. Adjusted for opponent defensive rating, home/away, score differential, and time remaining.
design.sample: All team-seasons from 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons (approximately 90 team-seasons).
design.power: With 90 units, a one-sided binomial test for proportion >0.7 at alpha=0.05 would have 60% power if the true proportion is 0.85, assuming independent observations. However, high variance in per-unit lift estimates (due to sparsity) will reduce power further; the effective sample may be insufficient.
design.controls: Linear regression of pull-up PPP on PNR-failure indicator, team-season fixed effects, opponent defensive rating, home/away, score margin bucket, period, and an interaction term to capture the counter lift. Include team-season average non-failure pull-up PPP as a covariate to reduce regression to the mean.
design.falsification: 1. Placebo test: replace PNR failure with a random negative outcome not known to trigger a counter (e.g., a block or a non-PNR missed shot); lift should not appear. 2. Test whether pull-up PPP after a successful PNR (scored on) shows a similar pattern. 3. Shuffle failure labels within team-seasons to generate a null distribution of the proportion-of-units statistic.
design.multiplicity: A single pre-specified test: one-sided binomial test that the proportion of team-seasons with positive adjusted lift exceeds 0.7. No per-unit hypothesis testing is conducted; the median lift is reported descriptively only.
design.decision_rule: Declare support for the claim if (a) the one-sided binomial p-value < 0.05, (b) median adjusted lift across team-seasons > 0.02, and (c) all placebo tests and robustness checks yield non-significant or negligible effects. Otherwise reject the claim.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular season play-by-play and derived play-type possession records from the NBA stats API and project graph database.

methodological_questions: How to define PNR failure?
How to define pull-up shot?
How to compute lift as a per-possession metric?
What are the appropriate units of analysis (e.g., team-season, game, defender)?
How to test the proportion of units with lift>0?
How to handle sparsity when pull-up attempts are rare after PNR failures?
How to control for confounders like shot quality, defender distance, game state?
How to ensure median lift>2pp is meaningful across units?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-05-23, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter, it should show lift>0 in >=70% of units with median lift>2pp.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

{"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["PNR failure", "pull-up shot", "counter strategy", "defensive suppression", "lift"], "methodological_questions": ["How to define PNR failure?", "How to define pull-up shot?", "How to compute lift as a per-possession metric?", "What are the appropriate units of analysis (e.g., team-season, game, defender)?", "How to test the proportion of units with lift>0?", "How to handle sparsity when pull-up attempts are rare after PNR failures?", "How to control for confounders like shot quality, defender distance, game state?", "How to ensure median lift>2pp is meaningful across units?"], "query": "Research question: If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter, it should show lift>0 in >=70% of units with median lift>2pp. Looking for prior studies on pick-and-roll failure leading to pull-up shots as a counter strategy, and any established methodological approaches for testing such counter-effectiveness claims."}}

reasoning_details.text:
We need to identify the research concepts and methodological questions. The question: "If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter, it should show lift>0 in >=70% of units with median lift>2pp." So it's about pick-and-roll (PNR) failure and pull-up shot as a counter. The area: defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid). So we need to retrieve historical evidence related to this hypothesis.

Research concepts: PNR failure, pull-up shot, counter strategy, lift (probably points per possession or something), league-wide consistency, median lift threshold. I'll extract: ["PNR failure", "pull-up shot", "counter strategy", "defensive suppression", "lift"]. Methodological questions: the requirement is about testing lift>0 in >=70% of units with median>2pp. So methodological questions: "how to define PNR failure", "how to define pull-up shot", "how to compute lift", "what are units (team, game, season?)", "how to test proportion of units with lift>0", "median lift calculation", "sample size considerations", "potential confounders". So I'll craft a query summarizing the task. I'll call retrieve_history with these concepts and questions.

I need to use the action: tool, tool: retrieve_history. The args must include research_concepts (list), methodological_questions (list), query (string). I'll produce that.

We need to analyze the research question: "If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter, it should show lift>0 in >=70% of units with median lift>2pp."

We have retrieved history with 10 study families. Relevant ones? The question involves "PNR fail" (pick-and-roll failure) and "PULL_UP" (pull-up shot) as a counter. The historical evidence includes several families about adaptation, scheme inference, and PPP lift. But none directly address this specific question. Let's examine each returned record:

- FAM:SF-APPA-001: A1 adaptation falsification tests. About PPP lift for adapters, wrong-way, no-signal teams. Not directly about PNR fail -> pull-up. However, it shows methodological issues: label error, selection/RTM. Outcome status "artifact" due to construction/selection/labelling flaw. So it's a cautionary tale: adaptation lift studies can produce artifacts.

- FAM:SF-APPS-058: Observed on-ball defensive scheme labels very low rates (14.9% and 3.3%), untestable. This suggests that labeling defensive schemes (like PNR coverage) from matchup/PBP data is difficult and low-yield. That could be relevant for defining "PNR fail" - we need to identify when a PNR fails, which might require scheme labels. So this is a failed approach: labeling coverage from available data is insufficient.

- FAM:SF12: A1 within-scheme re-test controlling early-third PPP selection. Inconclusive. Not directly about PNR fail->pull-up.

- FAM:SF13: Within-game did_adapt toward SHOULD counters improves PPP. They found adapters improve PPP. But outcome "artifact" due to selection/RTM. That's relevant: counter adaptation studies can produce spurious positive results due to regression to the mean. So methodology risk.

- FAM:SF27: Linear team+opponent+play_type baseline vs simulation kernel. Inconclusive, not about PNR fail.

- FAM:SF-PAP-098: Calibrated simulation vs Elo/net-rating/lineup+/- baselines, not a hypothesis test, artifact. Not relevant.

- FAM:SF-APPA-020: Evaluation-alignment diagnostic, not a hypothesis test, null result. Not relevant.

- FAM:SF-CHT-009: Superstar suppression by lineup and forced play type. Found that forced PULL_UP for Giannis is worse than preferred DRIVE. This touches on pull-up as a "forced" play type, but not in context of PNR failure. Related to counter effectiveness? Possibly, but outcome "not a hypothesis test". Risk: PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE. Not directly.

- FAM:SF-APPA-067, 066: TOV_FORCE studies, not relevant.

So the key historical evidence: several studies about adaptation lift and counter claims have been plagued by artifacts, labeling difficulties, small samples, and regression to the mean. The scheme labeling study (SF-APPS-058) shows that the available data cannot confidently label defensive schemes, which would be needed to identify PNR failures. Also, the adaptation lift studies (SF-APPA-001, SF13) showed that naive lift measures can produce spurious artifacts.

Now, for this research question, we need to define "PNR fail": does that mean the offensive PNR resulted in a turnover, missed shot, no points, or a defensive stop? And what constitutes failure? Probably a possession that ends without scoring, or an outcome below average. But the data: play-by-play, derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points). So we can identify possessions that started as a PNR (play type = PNR) and then see the points scored on that possession. Failure could be defined as points=0 or less than some threshold. But "fail" might also refer to the defense's success in stopping the PNR, like a forced turnover or bad shot. However, the research question states "If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter". That seems to mean: after a PNR fails (the offensive team does not score on that PNR possession), the offensive team then uses a pull-up shot as a counter strategy later in the game or maybe immediately after? The definition is ambiguous. Likely it's about the offensive team, when their PNR is stopped, they resort to pull-up jumpers. So the "counter" is that the offense shifts to using pull-up shots instead of PNR. So we need to define "lift": presumably the points per possession (PPP) of pull-up shots after a PNR failure compared to baseline. The claim is that across "units" (maybe team-season, defender, game), 70% of units show lift>0 and median lift across units > 2 percentage points.

So methodological questions: definition of PNR failure, definition of pull-up shot, unit of analysis, computing lift as PPP difference, testing the proportion of units with positive lift, handling sparsity, confounding.

Now, the historical evidence shows that previous attempts to measure counter adaptation using PPP lift have run into artifacts (selection/RTM, labeling error). The scheme labeling study shows that identifying PNR defense coverages from data is unreliable; but here we might not need coverage labels, we just need to know if a PNR possession failed (points scored = 0). That only requires play type and points, which are available from derived play-type possession records. So we can identify PNR possessions and their points. So labeling PNR coverages isn't required. However, the question of "PNR fail" might be confounded by shot quality, defense, etc.

The historical evidence does not directly answer the question, but it cautions against naive lift calculations. So we need to address risks: especially regression to the mean (RTM_SELECTION), because if we condition on a PNR failure (a negative event), subsequent pull-up PPP might regress upward, creating spurious positive lift. Also, sample size/power: pull-ups are a subset of play types; after PNR failures, pull-up attempts might be rare, leading to sparse data. Units might be too small for reliable lift estimation. Also, confounding: the team's overall offensive ability, opponent defense, game state, etc. Also, the definition of "lift" could be mechanically biased if we compare after-failure pull-up PPP to overall pull-up PPP without adjusting for opponent or situation.

The research question calls for a league-wide test: 70% of units must have lift>0, median lift>2pp. That's a strong claim. We need to define "units" appropriately. Possibilities: team-season (30 teams per season), or team-game (many games), or defender-against-team, etc. The question says "units" without specifying, so we need to choose. For power, if we use team-season, there would be at most 30 observations per season, too few for a reliable 70% proportion test if the effect is small and noisy. Team-game would yield many units but very low sample size per unit (few pull-ups after PNR failure per game). Defender-matchup would be even sparser.

So risks: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, CONFOUNDING, RTM_SELECTION, MECHANICAL_FLOOR (if floor effects cause upward bias), LABEL_ERROR (if pull-up definition is noisy), PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE (similar to other artifact findings), MULTIPLE_TESTING if many units tested.

Given historical evidence that similar counter-adaptation studies were artifacts, the predicted outcome probability heavily weighs artifact or untestable. I'd lean toward do_not_proceed due to high risk of artifact and sparsity.

But the task is to decide whether to proceed, with design, or not. I'll structure the output accordingly.

Now, I need to fill the schema. Let's collect historical_evidence from the relevant families: SF-APPA-001 (artifact, label error, RTM), SF-APPS-058 (untestable, low label rates, small sample), SF13 (artifact, RTM), SF12 (inconclusive). For failed_approaches: SF-APPS-058 (scheme labeling failure), SF-APPA-001 (adaptation lift artifact), SF13 (adaptation artifact due to RTM). Also SF-CHT-009 (forced pull-up study, but not failed approach? It's not a hypothesis test, but it found forced pull-up had negative impact, but that's not directly a failed approach for this question. Still, it indicates possible placebo dependence. I'll include relevant ones.

I need to cite identifiers exactly as recorded. For each historical_evidence, I'll pick those that show relevant findings. The most relevant are SF-APPA-001 (artifact) and SF-APPS-058 (untestable) because they highlight labeling and selection issues. Also SF13 (artifact). I'll list them.

For failed_approaches: SF-APPS-058 (labeling defensive schemes from matchup/PBP failed), SF-APPA-001 (adaptation lift study produced artifact due to selection/RTM), SF13 (adaptation lift artifact). Possibly SF27? Not failed, just inconclusive.

Evidence establishes: previous adaptation lift studies have been artifacts; scheme labeling from available data is unreliable; small sample sizes in similar studies. Evidence does not establish: that this specific PNR fail->pull-up counter cannot be tested; no prior study directly addressed this claim.

Own inferences: The question is testable in principle if we properly define failure and pull-up, but is at high risk of artifact due to regression to the mean and sparsity; the 70% threshold and 2pp median lift are very optimistic; they implicitly assume a strong effect, but the data may not support it.

Uncertainties: definition of "PNR fail" (points = 0, or below league average, or defensive stop?), definition of "units" (team-game, team-season, opponent?), appropriate baseline for lift (overall pull-up PPP, or pull-up PPP from similar game situations), how to handle possessions where a pull-up occurs immediately after PNR failure vs later in game.

Testability: I'd give a low p_testable, maybe 0.2, because sparsity and RTM are likely to make power low. Blocking constraints: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (units may have too few pull-ups after failure), EXPOSURE_SPARSITY (pull-up events rare), RTM_SELECTION (conditioning on failure leads to regression), CONFOUNDING (opponent, game state). Also LABEL_ERROR if pull-up definition is ambiguous.

Prior work: already_answered = "no", because no retrieved study addressed the same question. Cited: SF-APPA-001, SF-APPS-058, SF13, SF12 perhaps. But SF12 is inconclusive, not directly.

Risks: list the relevant risk codes.

Predicted outcome: I'd say supported: low (maybe 0.1), rejected: low (0.1), untestable: moderate (0.4), artifact: high (0.4) due to RTM, uncertain: low. Sum to 1.

Decision: do_not_proceed. I'll design a minimum viable test anyway.

Design: Estimand: difference in points per possession (PPP) between pull-up shots occurring after a PNR failure and a counterfactual baseline of pull-up shots in comparable situations not preceded by a PNR failure. Unit: team-season (or team-game, but I'll specify team-season to have more possessions per unit, but 30 per season is low for 70% test). Possibly use defender-team-season? I need to pick something that yields enough units. The claim is "league-wide", so we need many units. I'd suggest team-game as units, then aggregate proportion of positive lift across all team-games and median lift. That could give thousands of units, but each unit may have very few pull-ups after PNR failure, leading to high variance. Maybe team-season is more stable but only 30 per season. Could pool multiple seasons to get ~90 units, which might be enough to test 70% with some power. For lift, we could compute for each team-season the mean PPP of pull-ups after PNR failure vs mean PPP of all other pull-ups by that team in that season, then test if >0. The median lift across team-seasons should be >2pp. This could be powered if the effect is huge, but with RTM it will be small. So probably underpowered.

I'll design with multiple seasons, controlling for opponent defensive rating, game location, score differential, and using a regression adjustment to avoid RTM: compare pull-up PPP after failure to expected pull-up PPP given the same predictors, using a pre-failure model. That addresses RTM_SELECTION. Also use a placebo test: look at PPP after successful PNR possessions to see if pull-up lift similarly appears.

Falsification: placebo where "PNR success" (points>0) predicts pull-up lift; if lift exists there too, it's not a failure-specific counter.

Multiplicity: since we test proportion>70% across many units, need to account for multiple testing if doing per-unit hypothesis tests. But the claim is about a single summary statistic: proportion of units with positive lift. So we just need one test: whether the observed proportion is significantly greater than 0.7, possibly using a binomial test or bootstrap. Still, multiple units are used to compute that proportion, but no multiplicity correction needed for that. However, if we test per-unit significance, there would be multiple testing. So I'll specify that the test is based on all units, not per-unit.

Data version: use all available seasons for max power, but beware nonstationarity. Use cross-validation.

So decision do_not_proceed because artifacts from earlier similar studies suggest high risk of spurious positive lift, plus sparsity and low power. But I'll still outline a design.

Now, craft the JSON. Ensure all fields filled. I need to include historical_evidence and failed_approaches with proper IDs. Use the returned IDs exactly: "FAM:SF-APPA-001", etc. I'll list them with status as recorded: "artifact", "untestable", etc.

I'll include families: FAM:SF-APPA-001, FAM:SF-APPS-058, FAM:SF13, FAM:SF12? SF12 is inconclusive, but I'll skip if not needed. I'll use three.

Now, for historical_evidence: each object: id, status_as_recorded, finding. I'll summarize finding from record. For FAM:SF-APPA-001: "A1 adaptation falsification found adapter PPP lift +0.0667, but effect was artifact due to construction/selection/labelling flaw; wrong-way teams showed lift too, and scheme-confidence gradient was opposite." For FAM:SF-APPS-058: "Scheme labeling from matchup/PBP fields achieved only 14.9% and 3.3% confident label rates; untestable due to small sample and labeling error." For FAM:SF13: "Within-game adaptation to SHOULD counters improved PPP by +0.058, but later identified as artifact due to selection/regression to the mean."

For failed_approaches: same IDs with what_failed and why. For SF-APPS-058: "labeling defensive schemes from matchup/PBP data" failed because low label rates and missing switches. For SF-APPA-001: "naive adaptation PPP lift test" failed because artifact from construction/selection. For SF13: "adaptation toward counters PPP lift" failed due to regression to the mean.

Now, evidence_establishes: list what these show: adaptation lift studies in basketball have been susceptible to artifacts from regression to the mean and selection bias; labeling defensive conditions from play-by-play is unreliable; small sample sizes plague counter analysis. evidence_does_not_establish: that the PNR fail -> pull-up counter is untestable; no study directly tested that claim.
